argument: De Beauvoir extends Sartre's facticity/transcendence duality into a fuller thesis of 'the ambiguity of human existence': we are irreducibly both sides of many simultaneous dualities (subject/object, individual/collective, mind/matter), and historical philosophical and religious systems that collapse one side are, structurally, bad faith institutionalized at a cultural scale. Answering the relativism objection, she argues that freedom is not chosen but an inescapable structural fact -- Sartre's 'condemned to be free' -- which grounds ethics without appeal to objective good or evil, since moral accountability scales with the freedom actually available (the skateboard/semi-truck example) and 'you don't offer an ethics to a god' or to someone genuinely powerless. She then catalogs bad-faith personality types along a ladder of freedom, including the apathetic, mob-prone 'sub-man' and the most common type, the 'serious man,' who fills the lack in existence by attaching total, fixed identity to an external cause, arguing ultimately that meaning is never handed down but continuously chosen and enacted.
keyIdeas: De Beauvoir's 'ambiguity of human existence' extends beyond facticity/transcendence to many simultaneous dualities (subject/object, individual/collective, mind/matter, self/other); to be human is to be irreducibly both sides of each at once, producing permanent tension. Historical philosophical and religious systems (Platonic forms, mind/body dualism, nationalism) are strategies that oversimplify existence by collapsing one side -- structurally identical to individual bad faith, just institutionalized at a cultural scale.

Answering the relativism objection to existentialist ethics, de Beauvoir argues (via Sartre's 'condemned to be free') that freedom isn't chosen but is an inescapable structural fact of the human condition, giving ethics a non-arbitrary foundation without appeal to objective good or evil.

Moral accountability scales with the freedom actually available in a situation, as the skateboard/semi-truck thought experiment shows; correspondingly, 'you don't offer an ethics to a god' nor to someone who believes themselves wholly powerless.

The 'sub-man,' lowest on de Beauvoir's ladder of bad faith, is apathetic, believing nothing merits desire or effort -- denying any inner tension by disengaging, which makes him socially dangerous as malleable, mob-prone fodder for others' projects; the 'serious man,' the most common type, instead fills the ambiguity/lack by attaching total, permanent identity to an external cause, treating a chosen, revisable commitment as a fixed essence.

De Beauvoir's final argument is that meaning was never handed down cosmically -- it is continuously chosen and enacted, and you cannot escape having some meaning, since even declaring life meaningless (the nihilist's error, forgetting it is up to him to justify the world) is itself a meaning-making act.
